analysis.one_liner: Forces the EPA and Army Corps to withdraw their clean water rule and write a narrower replacement with mandatory state consultation.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 261-155 on May 12, 2015, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2015 the EPA and Army Corps proposed a rule defining which streams, wetlands, and ponds count as "waters of the United States" and therefore need federal protection and permits under the Clean Water Act. This bill would have forced the agencies to withdraw that rule within 30 days of enactment and start over, under a new process requiring consensus-style consultation with state and local officials, a detailed report, and at least 180 days of public comment. It would also have given states two years to bring their water permit programs into line with any new rule before the EPA could pull its approval.
analysis.who_benefits: Large farms, land developers, and energy and mining companies that would face fewer federal permits for filling or polluting small streams, ditches, and wetlands near their operations, plus state and local governments seeking more control over water permitting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large farms, developers, mining and energy companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Army Secretary and EPA Administrator to withdraw the 2014 proposed waters rule, and any final rule based on it, within 30 days of enactment.

Requires the agencies to write a new definition through joint consultation with state and local officials and stakeholders, producing a report on the consultations and detailed economic impact analyses, with at least 180 days for public review and comment.
Directs the agencies to recognize state primacy over water rights and land use and to incorporate areas where consensus was reached with the consulted state and local officials.
After any final rule, gives states a two-year grace period to bring noncompliant Clean Water Act permit programs into compliance before the EPA can withdraw its approval.

analysis.who_pays: People whose drinking water comes from small streams and wetlands, which would lose the clear federal protection the rule provided; downstream communities and fisheries that depend on those upstream waters; and the EPA and Army Corps, which would redo a rulemaking with no additional funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households drinking from upstream streams and wetlands

drawbacks.text: Withdrawing the rule would immediately strip defined federal protection from tributary streams and adjacent wetlands that feed public drinking water supplies, leaving permit decisions for those waters uncertain until a replacement rule is written.

The bill requires the new rule to incorporate the areas where consensus was reached with consulted state and local officials, a standard critics said could make any new rule impossible to finalize when states disagree with each other, and it authorizes no new funding for the redo.

Supporters' own case: the 2014 rule reached beyond the Supreme Court's Clean Water Act rulings, threatened to extend federal permitting to farmland ditches and low-value waters, and was written without adequate consultation with states, imposing real compliance costs on landowners.
A 180-day comment period, mandatory consensus consultations, and a comprehensive report would add years of delay before any replacement definition could take effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — more state input and a clearer definition — is a legitimate one, and the 2014 rule was genuinely contested in the courts. But the bill's design does not simply improve the rule; it cancels the existing protections first and rebuilds from scratch under a consensus requirement that could stall a replacement indefinitely, so during that stretch small streams and wetlands would have no clear federal safeguard. For people who drink water drawn from those sources, that is the cost; for regulated farms, developers, and extractive industries, avoided permitting is the gain.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote in May 2015, but the Senate let it sit — it wasn't even referred to committee until July 2016 — and it never got a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 13, 2015, the bill cleared the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on a 36-22 vote just two days after referral, and was reported as amended on April 27, 2015.

On May 12, 2015, a Democratic motion to recommit — which would have instructed the agencies to safeguard public water supplies including the Great Lakes, mitigate western drought, preserve irrigation water, and address flooding — failed 175-241, with all 237 voting Republicans opposed.
The House passed the bill 261-155 on May 12, 2015: Republicans voted 237-0 in favor, while Democrats split 24 in favor to 155 opposed.

The Senate received the bill on May 13, 2015, but did not refer it to the Environment and Public Works Committee until July 14, 2016, and it never received a Senate vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Clean Water Rule stayed on the books for the rest of that Congress, so people whose drinking water comes from small streams and wetlands kept protections the bill would have scrapped. Farms, developers, and extractive industries did not get the withdrawal and restart they had sought, though the rule itself remained tied up in litigation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water drinkers who kept the rule's protections

for.name: Bill Shuster
for.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through his committee, which reported it amended on a 36-22 vote, to the House floor within three weeks of introduction.

for.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the House
for.what_they_did: Marked the bill up on April 15, 2015, ordered it reported amended 36-22, and reported it on April 27, 2015.

for.name: 237 of 244 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 237-0, on May 12, 2015.

against.name: 155 of 188 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and unanimously supported a motion to recommit that would have required the replacement rule to protect public water supplies and address drought and flooding.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill after the House passed it, but only took the referral in July 2016, more than a year later, and the Senate never voted on the bill.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: The administration opposed the bill and its attempt to force withdrawal of the waters rule; Obama later vetoed a related attempt to nullify the rule through the Congressional Review Act.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split by party: every voting Republican (237 of 237) backed the bill, while 155 of 188 Democrats opposed it, with 24 Democrats crossing over to support it.

industries.note: Farm and ranch groups objected that the waters rule could subject ditches, ponds, and seasonal streams on farmland to federal permitting. The bill would have scrapped the rule and forced a consensus-based rewrite, removing the permitting threat during the process.
Developers face federal permits and delays when filling wetlands or streams on project sites. Withdrawing the rule would clear those requirements until any replacement rule is finalized.

industries.industry: Mining, oil and gas, and utilities with water discharges
industries.note: The rule's definition determines which waters near operations require discharge and dredge-and-fill permits. A narrower or absent definition reduces compliance costs and constraints on siting and construction.

industries.industry: Public drinking water systems and downstream communities
industries.note: The rule protected tributary streams and wetlands that feed public drinking water supplies. Withdrawing it first and replacing it later would leave those source waters without clear federal protection during the gap.

The bill would give states more say over water permitting and two years to adjust their programs before EPA could withdraw approval. But state water quality agencies would bear more permitting and program-compliance work with no new federal funding.
